Kerchief
KER-chif
noun
From the Old French couvrechief, “cover-head,” from couvrir (“to cover”) and chief (“head”); hence a cloth for the head. In Ezekiel it names the long veils the false prophetesses made and set upon the heads of their clients.

Biblical Definition

A kerchief is a cover for the head — the word is literally “cover-chief,” a cloth laid over the crown. In all Scripture it appears only in one dark chapter, and there it is an instrument of soul-hunting. Ezekiel is sent against the daughters of his people who prophesy out of their own heart: they sew pillows to all armholes and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls (Eze 13:18). Here is a trade in charms. The women fitted their wares to every customer — a kerchief for every stature, cut to the measure of the one who paid — and with soft cushions and covered heads they promised life to those the LORD had not quickened and death to those He had not condemned. The LORD’s answer is a tearing: “Your kerchiefs also will I tear, and deliver my people out of your hand, and they shall be no more in your hand to be hunted; and ye shall know that I am the LORD” (Eze 13:21). He is against their pillows and will let the hunted souls go free (Eze 13:20), until they see no more vanity nor divine divinations (Eze 13:23). The kerchief therefore stands for every religious article sold to the anxious — the covering that comforts the head while the soul goes unwarned. God tears such coverings off, and the tearing is mercy.

Webster 1828 Definition

A cloth for covering the head; in Ezekiel, the veils the false prophetesses made to hunt souls, which the LORD promised to tear.

KERCHIEF, a cloth to cover the head; literally “cover-chief.”

From Old French couvrechief, from couvrir, “to cover,” and chief, “head.”

It occurs in Scripture only of the false prophetesses of Ezekiel 13.

Made upon the head of every stature, cut to the measure of the buyer, to hunt souls.

The LORD promised to tear the kerchiefs and set the hunted souls free (Eze 13:21).

Key Scripture

Eze 13:21 — "Your kerchiefs also will I tear, and deliver my people out of your hand, and they shall be no more in your hand to be hunted; and ye shall know that I am the LORD."

Eze 13:20 — "Wherefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against your pillows, wherewith ye there hunt the souls to make them fly, and I will tear them from your arms, and will let the souls go, even the souls that ye hunt to make them fly."

Eze 13:23 — "Therefore ye shall see no more vanity, nor divine divinations: for I will deliver my people out of your hand: and ye shall know that I am the LORD."

Jer 23:16 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

A live corruption: the trade Ezekiel condemned is still open, and the modern market in prophetic words and holy trinkets hunts souls with kerchiefs of its own.

expand to see more

The corruption named here is not ancient but present. Ezekiel’s women prophesied out of their own heart and sold the comfort of it, fitting a kerchief to the head of every stature — and the same shop is open today. The self-appointed prophet who sells a word from the Lord, the anointed cloth mailed to the giver, the point-of-contact trinket, the prophetic conference where a vision of a man’s own heart is priced and delivered: these are kerchiefs. The dictionary is cessationist with the Reformed churches: the canon is closed, and no man now speaks new revelation. Deuteronomy sentences the prophet who presumes to speak a word the LORD has not commanded, and Jeremiah bids the people hearken not to prophets who make them vain. To take money for a word God never spoke is to hunt the souls of His people.

Mark what the kerchief actually does: it covers the head and leaves the soul unwarned. That is the whole art of the false prophetess — to lay something soft where God would lay conviction, to promise life to those He has not quickened and to slay the souls that should live. The faithful minister has no wares to sell and no covering to offer but Christ; he preaches the Word, and the Word wounds before it heals. And the LORD’s judgment upon the whole trade is a mercy to the hunted: “Your kerchiefs also will I tear, and deliver my people out of your hand.” He strips the covering to save the soul under it, and the delivered people know at last that He is the LORD.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a cloth for covering the head — literally a “cover-chief.”

expand to see more

Kerchief — Old French couvrechief, “cover-head.”

From couvrir, “to cover,” and chief, “head.”

It denotes a cloth laid over the crown of the head.

In Ezekiel it names the charm-veils of the false prophetesses.

The LORD tears the kerchief to free the hunted soul (Eze 13:21).

Usage

"They made kerchiefs upon the head of every stature — a charm cut to the measure of the buyer."

"Your kerchiefs also will I tear: God strips the covering to deliver the soul beneath it."

"Every prophetic word sold for money is a kerchief, and the trade hunts souls still."
